content: The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management: Guidelines on Pesticide Legislation was published in September 2015 by the World Health Organization (WHO) and the Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) of the United Nations. This document provides a comprehensive framework for the regulation and management of pesticides, aiming to protect public health and the environment while ensuring the safe and effective use of these substances. The guidelines emphasize that reproduction and dissemination of the material for educational or non-commercial purposes are permitted without prior written permission, provided the source is fully acknowledged. However, reproduction for resale or commercial purposes requires written authorization from the copyright holders. The document also clarifies that the designations and presentation of material do not imply any opinion on the legal or developmental status of any country, territory, or area. The regulatory framework for pesticide control includes a wide range of legislation, such as those governing environmental protection, public health, occupational health, water safety, food safety, wildlife conservation, marine protection, plant protection, and general chemical management. It also incorporates obligations under international agreements. Pesticide legislation specifically refers to legal instruments designed to regulate pesticides, including primary instruments like laws or acts and secondary instruments like regulations or decrees. The primary pesticide law establishes the core principles, mandates, and responsibilities for pesticide management and typically requires parliamentary approval. Secondary legislation, such as regulations, provides detailed rules for specific areas of pesticide control and can often be issued at the ministerial level. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, first adopted by FAO in 1985, has undergone several revisions to address evolving needs. It was amended in 1989 to include the Prior Informed Consent (PIC) procedure, revised in 2002, and updated in 2013 to include public health pesticides. WHO adopted the Code in 2014 as its reference framework for international guidance on pesticide management. Since the Code's initial adoption, several international instruments related to pesticide management have come into force, including the Rotterdam Convention, the Stockholm Convention, the Basel Convention, the Montreal Protocol, and the International Labour Organization (ILO) Convention No. 184 on Safety and Health in Agriculture. Other developments include the Strategic Approach to International Chemicals Management (SAICM) and the Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS). While significant progress has been made in pesticide legislation globally, many existing laws have weaknesses. These may include outdated penalties, unclear enforcement authority, or insufficient alignment with international agreements and regional initiatives. Additionally, institutional changes and new mandates may not have been adequately addressed, leading to inconsistencies and gaps in regulatory frameworks. Governments regulate pesticides to protect human health, the environment, and ensure the effectiveness of pesticide products. This includes safeguarding pesticide users, consumers, the public, crops, livestock, wildlife, and water bodies. Legislation also aims to ensure fair markets for manufacturers, importers, and distributors. Effective pesticide management requires not only legislation but also institutional infrastructure, supporting policies, and tools to promote sustainable pest and pesticide management. The guidelines recommend promoting Integrated Pest Management (IPM) and Integrated Vector Management (IVM) through training programs, incentives, and the use of low-risk products. Public education campaigns, scientific research, and training for inspectors and professional users are also essential. A robust legislative framework should underpin these efforts. The document supersedes the 1989 Guidelines for Legislation on the Control of Pesticides and refers to technical guidelines published by FAO and WHO for specific elements of pesticide legislation. FAO also maintains a repository of national legislation relevant to agriculture, including pesticide laws, which can serve as references for countries. Governments are encouraged to introduce policies and legislation for the regulation of pesticides throughout their lifecycle, ensuring effective coordination and enforcement. This includes establishing educational, advisory, extension, and healthcare services based on FAO and WHO guidelines and relevant legally binding instruments. Additionally, legislation should prevent the use and sale of pesticides to children, as recommended by the International Partnership for Cooperation on Child Labour in Agriculture. Monitoring pesticide use in local contexts can provide insights for further developing regulatory frameworks. Existing national pesticide legislation may need updating to address changes in regulatory and institutional frameworks, new needs, and applicable international or regional standards. Inconsistencies within regulatory frameworks often arise from varying definitions, overlapping mandates, and conflicting provisions. These issues may result from uncoordinated development of laws or ad hoc responses to specific problems. FAO and WHO encourage governments to integrate ministerial responsibilities for pesticide regulation into a single pesticide law that applies to all pesticides. This approach minimizes administrative duplication and gaps in coverage, ensuring a more cohesive and effective regulatory system.
